instrument: International Plant Protection Convention (IPPC)
description: Aims to prevent the introduction and spread of plant pests across borders while facilitating safe trade. Establishes standards for phytosanitary measures, encourages harmonization, and creates a framework for international surveillance, certification, and response.
principles: Equity: Reinforces equitable responsibilities across countries through harmonized plant health measures.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Aims to preserve ecological balance by preventing the spread of invasive plant pests.
Stewardship: Emphasizes prevention over reaction, promoting long-term environmental stewardship.
Transdisciplinarity: Facilitates cross-sectoral and intergovernmental collaboration through regional organizations.
governanceRole: Legally binding framework for coordinated global plant health governance; harmonized international standards and surveillance systems; integrates plant health with trade, food security, and environmental protection.
limitations: No binding obligations on environmental monitoring or climate-related plant risks. Collaboration with other One Health instruments is not formally structured.
provisions: Preamble: Takes into account principles governing protection of plant, human, animal health, and environment. Article VIII(1): Cooperation on pest information exchange. Article XX: Provision of technical assistance.
interlinkages: WTO Agreement on Sanitary and Phytosanitary Measures (SPS)

instrument: International Convention for Protection of New Plant Varieties (UPOV)
description: Provides an effective system of plant variety protection to encourage development of new varieties, granting breeders exclusive rights.
principles: Equity: Provides benefits to breeders and farmers alike.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Supports crop innovation for environmental challenges.
Stewardship: Ensures future food security and sustainability.
Transdisciplinarity: Interdisciplinary collaboration between science, agri-business, and farmers.
governanceRole: Allows use of protected varieties for breeding new varieties (Breeder's Exemption). Supports climate change adaptation and capacity building for agricultural productivity.
limitations: Implementation challenges regarding testing requirements for low-resource countries. Strong breeders' rights may influence access for farmers or researchers.
provisions: Article 15(1)(iii): Breeders' Exemption. Article 15(2): Farmer's Privilege to save/reuse seeds. Article 17: Public Interest Exception.
interlinkages: Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), Nagoya Protocol

instrument: Convention on Wetlands (Ramsar Convention)
description: Establishes a global framework for wise use and conservation of wetlands. Parties must designate sites, maintain ecological character, and monitor changes.
principles: Equity: Promotes equity by conserving wetlands vital to human-animal-environment alike.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Supports biodiversity and socio-ecological equilibrium.
Stewardship: Encourages stewardship and sustainable use of shared ecosystems.
Transdisciplinarity: Encourages multisectoral governance via national focal points, COP bodies, and public participation.
governanceRole: Mandated ecological monitoring and reporting. Infrastructure for cooperation via COP and STRP. Wise-use principle offering flexible implementation.
limitations: Broad obligations without binding enforcement mechanisms. Variation in implementation of 'wise use'. Limited explicit reference to human health.
provisions: Article 1: Defines wetlands broadly. Article 2: Designate Ramsar sites. Article 3: Plan for conservation/wise use. Article 8: International cooperation.

instrument: Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES)
description: Regulates international trade in wildlife to ensure survival of vulnerable species via Appendices and permitting systems.
principles: Equity: Shared wildlife heritage.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Prevents biodiversity loss.
Stewardship: Humans as stewards of wildlife.
Transdisciplinarity: International cooperation for enforcement.
governanceRole: Reduces risk of zoonotic disease emergence via reporting on pathogen spillover in trade. Collaborates with WOAH. Permitting system regulates human-animal contact points.
limitations: Limited scope focused on trade rather than broad ecosystem health. Relies on national resource availability for implementation.
provisions: Article III(2)(c) & VIII(3): Safe transport of live specimens to minimize injury or damage to health. Article III(3)(b): Suitable housing requirements.

instrument: Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species (CMS)
description: Provides framework to restore or maintain favorable conservation status of migratory species by protecting habitats, regulating use, and fostering regional agreements.
principles: Equity: Protects species and habitats across all Parties for equitable ecosystem benefit.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Promotes socio-ecological balance by conserving migratory habitats.
Stewardship: Emphasizes stewardship via habitat restoration and species protection.
Transdisciplinarity: Advances transdisciplinarity through COP and agreements involving health/environment sectors.
governanceRole: Multisectoral surveillance and rapid risk response for wildlife health. Framework for cooperation via MoUs. Global data-sharing platforms.
limitations: Fragmented adoption of regional agreements. Enforcement gaps due to varying national capacities. Public health referenced only indirectly.
provisions: Art. 2: Obliges protection of species. Art. 3: Prohibits specified take/trade. COP Resolutions address wildlife health, zoonoses, and biosecurity.

instrument: United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS)
description: Comprehensive legal framework governing all uses of the world's oceans, establishing state rights/duties, and regulating marine environmental protection and resources.
principles: Equity: Affirms equitable sharing of ocean resources and special requirements of developing states.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Requires conservation to maintain populations and protect fragile ecosystems.
Stewardship: Imposes a binding duty to protect and preserve the marine environment.
Transdisciplinarity: Mandates global and regional cooperation for environmental standards.
governanceRole: Binding legal framework for marine environmental protection. Mandatory monitoring and transboundary notification. Conservation of aquatic resources.
limitations: Limited direct integration with human/animal health systems. Enforcement relies heavily on flag state compliance.
provisions: Article 192: Obligation to protect marine environment. Article 194(5): Protect rare ecosystems. Article 196: Prevent introduction of alien species.
interlinkages: Aquatic Animal Health Code, CBD, GBF, Ramsar

instrument: Basel Convention on the Control of Transboundary Movements of Hazardous Wastes
description: Aims to control transboundary movement and management of hazardous wastes. Regulates export/import, prevents illegal dumping, and promotes waste risk reduction.
principles: Equity: Helps low-income countries prevent illegal dumping and environmental injustice.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Reduces toxic exposures that disrupt ecosystems, biodiversity, and food systems.
Stewardship: Embodies stewardship through waste minimization and safe disposal.
Transdisciplinarity: Fosters multisectoral engagement through obligations on monitoring and reporting.
governanceRole: Reduces shared health risks from waste pollution. Supports national system strengthening for waste governance. Promotes international cooperation.
limitations: Focus primarily on waste management rather than broader health pathways. Variation in enforcement across contexts.
provisions: Article 4: Prohibits export/import of hazardous waste without informed consent. Article 5: Designate national authorities. Article 10: Technical assistance.

instrument: Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD)
description: Provides an overarching framework on biodiversity targeting conservation, sustainable use, and fair/equitable sharing of genetic resources.
principles: Equity: Promotes fair benefit sharing.
Inclusion: Acknowledges Indigenous knowledge and marginalized voices.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Emphasizes biodiversity balance.
Stewardship: Encourages sustainable use for the future.
Transdisciplinarity: Supports multisector programs.
governanceRole: Adopted Global One Health Policy for pandemic prevention. WHO-CBD collaboration on monitoring. Risk management tools and equity focus.
limitations: Many health components remain voluntary. Lack of binding provisions to harmonize multi-sector legislation. Monitoring indicators still in development.
provisions: Article 8: In-situ conservation and managing LMO risks. Article 14: Environmental impact assessments. Article 15: Access to genetic resources.

instrument: Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety
description: Protocol to the CBD ensuring safe transport, handling, and use of living modified organisms (LMOs) that may adversely affect biodiversity and human health.
principles: Equity: Capacity building for developing countries.
Inclusion: Public participation in country.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Protects biodiversity and health.
Stewardship: Precautionary responsibility.
Transdisciplinarity: International scientific cooperation.
governanceRole: Risk assessment guidance for LMOs. Biosafety Clearing-House for information sharing. Health-related indicators in reporting.
limitations: Primary emphasis on environmental impacts may not fully encompass human/animal health. Risk guidelines are non-binding. Resource constraints.
provisions: Article 1: Precautionary approach. Article 15: Risk assessment considering biodiversity and human health. Article 16: Risk management.
interlinkages: Codex Principles for Foods Derived from Modern Biotechnology

instrument: Nagoya Protocol on Access to Genetic Resources
description: Protocol to the CBD providing a transparent legal framework for fair and equitable benefit-sharing arising from the utilization of genetic resources.
principles: Equity: Fair and equitable sharing of benefits from genetic resources.
Inclusion: Addresses rights of indigenous/local communities, ensuring prior informed consent.
Transdisciplinarity: Encourages collaboration across research, public health, and industry.
governanceRole: Framework for equitable benefit-sharing supporting health equity. ABS Clearing-House for info exchange. Capacity building for developing countries.
limitations: Varied national implementation of ABS legislation. Complex administrative processes for authorization. Legal uncertainty regarding scope interpretation.
provisions: Article 8(b): Expeditious access to resources for health emergencies. Article 9: Benefits toward conservation. Article 12: Traditional knowledge benefit-sharing.

instrument: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)
description: Framework for intergovernmental efforts to tackle climate change, committing Parties to limit emissions and develop responses protecting vulnerable populations.
principles: Equity: Frames climate change as cross-sectoral requiring broad coordination.
Inclusion: Common but differentiated responsibilities explicitly recognizes inequality.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Recognizes adverse effects on ecosystems and links environmental stability to well-being.
Stewardship: Calls to protect climate system for present and future generations.
Transdisciplinarity: Calls for scientific cooperation, information exchange, and coordination.
governanceRole: Established a Health Programme (COP26). Multisectoral agricultural initiatives. Operationalized Loss and Damage Fund. Emphasizes climate-health knowledge sharing.
limitations: Slow progress on mitigation. Finance gaps. Health is not a central component of core climate negotiations. Varied national reporting.
provisions: Article 1: Defines adverse effects including human health. Article 2: Objective to stabilize GHG levels. Article 4.1: Adaptation planning and minimizing impacts.
interlinkages: WHO Pandemic Agreement, Paris Agreement, UNCCD

instrument: Paris Agreement
description: Agreement under UNFCCC aiming to limit global temperature rise via nationally determined contributions (NDCs).
principles: Equity: Just transitions and financing for the poor.
Inclusion: Indigenous and human rights.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Limits warming for ecosystems.
Stewardship: Intergenerational equity.
Transdisciplinarity: All nations meant to contribute.
governanceRole: Encourages inclusive adaptation planning (Article 7.9). Glasgow Climate Pact emphasizes integrated health-climate approaches. Enhances capacity building and knowledge sharing.
limitations: Limited explicit health focus. Implementation relies on voluntary NDC fulfillment. Resource constraints for climate-related health measures.
provisions: Article 7: Enhancing adaptive capacity to protect people/ecosystems via participatory approaches. Article 8: Building resilience regarding loss and damage.

instrument: United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD)
description: Legally binding agreement focused on land degradation and desertification. Promotes sustainable land management, ecosystem restoration, and climate resilience.
principles: Equity: Prioritizes rural/dryland communities facing degradation and health vulnerability.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Advances balance through land restoration and biodiversity conservation.
Stewardship: Supports long-term intergenerational responsibility for land/water.
Transdisciplinarity: Fosters collaboration between agriculture, climate, health, and indigenous knowledge.
governanceRole: Recognizes biodiversity loss links to spillover/malnutrition. Promotes integrated land management balancing ecosystems and livelihoods. Strengthens funding mechanisms.
limitations: Health impacts are implied but not explicitly embedded in operational provisions. Implementation gaps due to limited national resources.
provisions: Article 2: Mitigating drought as a global priority. Article 10: National Action Programmes for integrated land management. Article 16: Science and traditional knowledge.

instrument: WTO Agreement on Sanitary and Phytosanitary Measures (SPS)
description: Sets rules for food safety and animal/plant health standards in international trade. Allows science-based standards while preventing arbitrary barriers.
principles: Equity: Promotes scientific fairness in trade.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Prevents spread of pests/disease for animal and human health.
Stewardship: Responsibility to protect health as a dimension of well-being.
Transdisciplinarity: Veterinary, plant, and health sectors must collaborate.
governanceRole: Science-based approach (Article 2.2). Harmonization utilizing international standards. Capacity building for developing nations. Transparency in measures.
limitations: Harmonization across diverse contexts is complex. Some countries face ongoing resource constraints for SPS implementation.
provisions: Annex A: SPS measures cover risks from animal/plant diseases. Article 3: Harmonization with Codex/WOAH/IPPC. Article 5: Precautionary provisional measures allowed.

instrument: Rotterdam Convention on the Prior Informed Consent Procedure
description: Promotes shared responsibility in trade of hazardous chemicals. Establishes Prior Informed Consent procedure for exports, enhancing transparency and reducing health/environmental risks.
principles: Equity: Enables importing countries to make informed decisions over hazardous imports.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Reduces flow of pesticides/pollutants that destabilize ecosystems.
Stewardship: Advances precautionary management and transparent risk sharing.
Transdisciplinarity: Fosters collaboration between agriculture, health, trade, and environment.
governanceRole: Empowers countries to prevent harmful chemical exposures across species. Builds multisectoral chemical governance capacity. Mandates science-based decision-making.
limitations: Health sector leadership varies. Listing processes involve multiple steps and time. Non-compliance challenges due to differing national capacities.
provisions: Article 5: Process for listing banned chemicals. Article 10: Import decisions transparently communicated. Article 14: Mandates information exchange among parties.

instrument: Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs)
description: Protects human health and the environment from bioaccumulating, persistent chemicals. Aims to eliminate/restrict POPs linked to cancer, immune disruption, etc.
principles: Equity: Requires international cooperation to support low/middle-income countries.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Aims to restore equilibrium by eliminating disruptive toxic substances.
Stewardship: Embodies stewardship via lifecycle approaches to chemical use.
Transdisciplinarity: Reinforces transdisciplinary collaboration across sectors.
governanceRole: Links ecosystem health to human/animal health through binding controls. Strengthens national capacity for chemical risk governance. Drives international cooperation.
limitations: Sectoral focus limits explicit One Health integration. Differences in national monitoring and regulatory systems. Cross-sector coordination mechanisms lack definition.
provisions: Article 3: Bans/restricts highly toxic chemicals. Article 5: Targets unintentional POPs releases from combustion. Article 11: Promotes collaborative research/monitoring.

instrument: International Health Regulations
description: Framework for international management of public health risks and emergencies. Requires reporting of significant events and capacity building.
principles: Equity: Helping weaker health systems.
Inclusion: Non-discrimination in control measures.
Stewardship: Shared responsibility to prevent and control public health risks.
Transdisciplinarity: Requires whole-of-government approach.
governanceRole: Enhanced early warning system. Mandates One Health multisectoral collaboration. Capacity building for developing nations. States Parties Committee supports compliance.
limitations: Resource constraints in meeting core capacities. Sovereignty considerations may lead to varied implementation during emergencies.
provisions: Article 2: Prevent/control disease spread without unnecessary trade interference. Article 6: 24-hour notification for PHEIC. Article 14: Collaboration with FAO/WOAH.

instrument: Minamata Convention on Mercury
description: Global treaty to protect human health and environment from anthropogenic emissions of mercury, including lifecycle measures.
principles: Equity: Promotes equity by helping countries implement safe mercury alternatives.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Seeks equilibrium by reducing contamination of aquatic systems and food webs.
Stewardship: Requires parties to eliminate unnecessary mercury use and emissions.
Transdisciplinarity: Fosters cooperation among environmental, health, and industrial sectors.
governanceRole: Limits cross-species neurotoxic exposure. Mandates national implementation plans linking environmental and health authorities. Supports technology transfer.
limitations: Informal sectors (artisanal gold mining) are hard to regulate. Phasing out timelines vary based on national capacity.
provisions: Article 4: Phases out mercury-added products. Article 7: Targets ASGM mercury use. Article 16: Encourages strategies to protect vulnerable populations.

instrument: WHO Pandemic Agreement
description: Comprehensive global framework for pandemic prevention, preparedness, and response with equity as a core principle. Explicitly integrates a One Health approach (Article 5).
principles: Equity: Advances equity by ensuring support for developing countries and access to countermeasures.
Inclusion: Strengthens inclusion of communities and Indigenous Peoples in decision-making.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Promotes socio-ecological balance by addressing environmental drivers of disease.
Stewardship: Embodies stewardship through collaborative prevention protecting ecosystems.
Transdisciplinarity: Establishes multisectoral collaboration across health, veterinary, and environment.
governanceRole: Prioritizes equity. Mandates One Health integration. Creates pathogen access/benefit-sharing systems. Establishes COP.
limitations: Sovereignty clauses may influence coordinated global implementation. Resource dependence. Annex timing delays details. Non-binding implementation mechanism.
provisions: Article 4: Pandemic surveillance. Article 5: One Health approach. Article 12: Pathogen Access and Benefit-Sharing System. Article 18: Sustainable financing.

instrument: Terrestrial Animal Health Code
description: International standards for disease prevention, zoonoses, and AMR control. Recognized reference standard under the WTO SPS Agreement.
principles: Equity: Promotes collaboration between veterinary, public health, and environmental sectors.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Establishes guidelines accounting for the interconnectedness of animal, human, and environment.
Stewardship: Encourages responsible animal health management.
Transdisciplinarity: Aligns veterinary, trade, and public health policies for a holistic approach.
governanceRole: Comprehensive global standards. Supports cross-sectoral collaboration. Facilitates trade while ensuring health protection. Enhances surveillance/reporting.
limitations: Limited integration with environmental governance. Low-income countries struggle with recommended infrastructure capacities.
provisions: Chapter 1.1: Notification of animal diseases. Chapter 6.2: Role of veterinary services in food safety. Chapter 6.10: Prudent use of antimicrobials.

instrument: Rio Declaration on Environment and Development
description: Establishes 27 principles for sustainable development, affirming sovereign rights alongside responsibility to prevent transboundary environmental harm.
principles: Equity: Affirms common but differentiated responsibilities and priority for developing countries.
Inclusion: Recognizes the role of women, youth, Indigenous peoples, and local communities.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Frames sustainable development as requiring harmony between humans and nature.
Stewardship: Calls to reduce unsustainable patterns and act as Earth stewards.
Transdisciplinarity: Promotes international cooperation and cross-sectoral collaboration.
governanceRole: Normative foundation for environment-health integration. Provides equity framework for One Health governance. Establishes transboundary notification obligations.
limitations: Non-binding and declaratory. Limited direct health framing; depends on interpretation through subsequent instruments.
provisions: Principle 1: Entitlement to a healthy/productive life. Principle 4: Environmental protection integral to development. Principle 15: Precautionary approach.

instrument: Aquatic Animal Health Code
description: International standards supporting the health of aquatic animals and disease control in aquatic trade.
principles: Equity: Integrates fishery, aquaculture, and veterinary expertise.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Promotes biodiversity-conscious disease management.
Stewardship: Supports responsible aquaculture to prevent disease spillover and AMR.
Transdisciplinarity: Strengthens coordination between public health, fisheries, and environmental agencies.
governanceRole: Provides standards for aquatic disease control. Supports a One Health approach recognizing links to food/human health. Encourages sustainable biosecurity.
limitations: Gaps in environmental regulation integration. Challenges for small-scale/informal aquaculture in meeting standards.
provisions: Chapter 1.4: Aquatic animal health surveillance. Chapter 6.1: Recommendations for controlling AMR. Chapter 4.4: Disinfection protocols.

instrument: The International Code of Conduct on Pesticide Management
description: Voluntary framework for entities managing pesticides throughout their lifecycle. Promotes Integrated Pest Management and targets vulnerable groups' protection.
principles: Equity: Promotes equitable access to safe pesticide management for developing countries.
Inclusion: Identifies vulnerable groups and calls for legislative protection.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Calls for biodiversity protection and IPM/IVM to reduce agroecosystem disruption.
Stewardship: Embeds stewardship via a lifecycle approach and manufacturer responsibility.
Transdisciplinarity: Calls for coordinated action across governments, industry, academia, and civil society.
governanceRole: Establishes shared responsibilities across sectors. Strengthens national regulatory systems and surveillance capacity. Promotes IPM/IVM.
limitations: Variable implementation across countries. Relies on self-reporting with no formal compliance verification mechanism.
provisions: Article 1.4: Shared responsibility. Article 5.1: Reducing health/environmental risks via surveillance. Article 3.12: Resistance management.
interlinkages: Rotterdam, Stockholm, Basel, Codex, CBD, ILO Convention 182

instrument: Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction
description: Outlines targets and priorities to prevent/reduce disaster risks and losses in lives, livelihoods, and health.
principles: Equity: Focus on impact to vulnerable communities.
Inclusion: Inclusive approach for all of society.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Promotes resilience of ecosystems and society.
Stewardship: Risk reduction for future generations.
Transdisciplinarity: Multi-sector and multi-level responses.
governanceRole: Promotes multisectoral disaster risk governance. Calls for enhancing health system resilience in cooperation with IHR. Promotes ecosystem approaches.
limitations: Primary emphasis is disaster risk rather than deep One Health integration. Ongoing implementation challenges in developing countries. Fragmented coordination.
provisions: Para 15: All-hazards scope includes biological hazards. Priority 3: Resilient health systems. Priority 2 & 4: Coherence with IHR and One Health.

instrument: WHO Global Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance
description: Framework for national action to combat AMR, emphasizing the One Health approach across human, animal, and agricultural sectors.
principles: Equity: Access to effective antibiotics for all.
Inclusion: Engaging farmers and communities.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Addresses AMR in the environment.
Stewardship: Antibiotic stewardship.
Transdisciplinarity: Explicitly mentions One Health coordination.
governanceRole: Promotes multisectoral collaboration. Focuses on capacity building via surveillance. Provides implementation blueprint for National Action Plans. Global coordination.
limitations: Low global implementation of action plans. Severe resource and financing constraints. Fragmented governance. Environmental dimension is underrepresented.
provisions: Objective 4: Optimize antimicrobial use. Multisectoral Collaboration: Calls for integrated AMR surveillance and public awareness campaigns with FAO and OIE.
interlinkages: Codex texts on Foodborne AMR, WOAH Strategy on AMR

instrument: WOAH Strategy on Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR)
description: Supports WOAH Members to confront the threat of AMR in animals and humans, providing a framework for responsible antimicrobial use and surveillance.
principles: Equity: Encourages collaboration across human, animal, and environmental health sectors.
Stewardship: Advocates for responsible antimicrobial use to protect ecosystems.
Transdisciplinarity: Promotes integrated efforts among various disciplines.
governanceRole: Facilitates international cooperation and information sharing. Promotes antimicrobial stewardship in veterinary medicine. Integrates environmental dimensions.
limitations: Implementation challenges due to varying member resources. Gaps in environmental surveillance and ecosystem monitoring.
provisions: Awareness and Education on AMR risks. Advocates integrated surveillance and research. Encourages good governance and capacity building in veterinary services.
interlinkages: Codex texts on Foodborne AMR, WHO Global Action Plan on AMR

instrument: WHA 72(9) WHO global strategy on health, environment and climate change
description: Sets a transformative agenda to reduce deaths linked to environmental factors by 2030, calling for primary prevention and cross-sectoral policy integration.
principles: Equity: Empowers health sector to collaborate with other sectors on health determinants.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Addresses climate change, biodiversity loss, and pollution.
Stewardship: Calls for prevention-focused governance and environmentally sound policies.
Transdisciplinarity: Promotes 'Health in All Policies' and co-developed cross-sector monitoring.
governanceRole: Mainstreams environmental health into public health leadership. Creates formal platforms for cross-sector coordination. Promotes integrated surveillance.
limitations: One Health framing is underdeveloped operationally. Does not create shared governance structures with environmental partners.
provisions: Objective 1: One Health approach for AMR. Objective 4: Efficient cross-sectoral governance. Objective 5: Targeted environmental monitoring linked to public health.
interlinkages: UNFCCC, Paris Agreement, Global Action Plan on Climate Change and Health

instrument: Codex Code of Practice to Minimize and Contain Foodborne AMR
description: Supports governments tackling foodborne AMR by addressing responsible antimicrobial use across the food chain, from production to retail.
principles: Equity: Ensures AMR strategies benefit human and animal health.
Inclusion: Requires global cooperation in regulation.
Stewardship: Prudent antimicrobial use.
Transdisciplinarity: Integrates veterinary, agricultural, and public health.
governanceRole: Requires cross-sectoral coordination on AMR. Prompts inclusion into national AMR action plans. Promotes integrated food, animal, and human surveillance.
limitations: Scope challenges as human healthcare/environment sectors are outside Codex. Low-resource settings face implementation capacity issues.
provisions: Principles 1-4, 6, 16: One Health priority approaches. Section 5: Responsible/prudent use of agents along food chain. Section 7: Consumer risk communication.
interlinkages: WTO SPS, WHO Global Action Plan on AMR, WOAH AMR Strategy

instrument: Codex General Standard for Contaminants and Toxins in Food and Feed
description: Sets general principles and maximum levels for chemical contaminants and natural toxins in foods and animal feeds to protect public health and ensure fair trade.
principles: Inclusion: Addresses environmental contaminants in food production.
Stewardship: Promotes risk management to prevent chemical contamination.
Transdisciplinarity: Integrates environmental, agricultural, and food safety sciences.
governanceRole: Fosters collaboration among food, agriculture, and environmental authorities. Facilitates trade and harmonized global data exchange.
limitations: Requires extensive inter-sector monitoring capacity. Doesn't cover pesticides or veterinary drugs. High testing burdens for low-resource settings.
provisions: Section 1.3: Applies to contaminants impacting health. Section 3: Establishes Maximum Levels to prevent toxic exposures.

instrument: General Principles of Food Hygiene
description: Provides foundational food hygiene practice codes applicable throughout the food chain to prevent contamination, establishing GHPs and HACCP systems.
principles: Equity: Universal hygiene standards across all food sectors.
Inclusion: Requires safe water use and proper waste management.
Stewardship: Promotes sustainable hygiene practices.
Transdisciplinarity: HACCP integrates multiple food safety disciplines.
governanceRole: Engages producers, veterinary professionals, and regulators. International adoption harmonizes safety measures to protect health/trade.
limitations: Focuses primarily on food handling, rarely explicitly engaging environmental authorities. Capacity concerns for small farms implementing HACCP.
provisions: Section 3: Primary Production contamination control. Section 5: Control of Operation via HACCP-based controls.

instrument: Decision 15/4: Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework
description: Post-2020 global strategy to halt/reverse biodiversity loss by 2030, explicitly embedding biodiversity-health interlinkages and One Health approaches.
principles: Equity: Affirms equity for Indigenous Peoples, LMICs, and intergenerational justice.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Frames biodiversity as foundational determinant of health.
Stewardship: Centers nature-based solutions and sustainable resource use.
Transdisciplinarity: Formalizes whole-of-society cooperation.
governanceRole: Elevates biodiversity-health linkages globally. Integrates these into spatial planning/food systems. Anchors equity/inclusive participation.
limitations: No standalone One Health indicator. Health ministries are not explicitly included in governance mandates.
provisions: Section C(r): Recognizes One Health principles. Goal B/Target 11: Elevates ecosystem services. Targets 4-7: Address zoonotic risk/pollution. Targets 14/21-23: Cross-sector coordination.

instrument: One Health Joint Plan of Action
description: Joint strategy by the Quadripartite outlining six action tracks addressing zoonoses, AMR, food safety, environment, and endemic disease burdens.
principles: Equity: Equity and fairness across all sectors in governance.
Inclusion: Inclusion of Indigenous/local communities, gender, and youth.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Emphasizes balance via biodiversity protection and ecosystem health.
Stewardship: Promotes proactive environmental management and AMR stewardship.
Transdisciplinarity: Grounded in transdisciplinary collaboration across policy and academia.
governanceRole: Anchors a global shared implementation structure. Provides roadmap tools for national adoption. Defines Theory of Change and robust M&E framework.
limitations: Limited uptake in several continents regarding the development of specific strategic plans.
provisions: Part 2: Theory of Change. Part 3: Six Action Tracks with deliverables. Part 4: Governance and M&E via Quadripartite. Part 5: Resource Mobilization.

instrument: MRLs and Risk Management Recommendations for Residues of Veterinary Drugs
description: Compendium listing Maximum Residue Limits (MRLs) and Risk Management Recommendations for veterinary drugs in animal-derived foods.
principles: Inclusion: Links veterinary drug use to environmental safety.
Stewardship: Enforces responsible veterinary drug practices.
Transdisciplinarity: Requires cooperation between veterinary and food safety regulators.
governanceRole: Harmonized international benchmark encouraging regulatory cooperation. Promotes joint surveillance and cross-agency enforcement.
limitations: Capacity constraints for enforcement in LMICs. Focuses strictly on consumer health rather than environmental/occupational exposure. Finite list of evaluated drugs.
provisions: Section 2: Defines Maximum Residue Limits. Annex: Risk Management Recommendations for prohibited drugs.

instrument: Decision 16/19: Global Action Plan for Biodiversity and Health
description: Adopts the GAP on Biodiversity and Health, supporting the GBF, recognizing biodiversity as a determinant of health and outlining voluntary actions.
principles: Equity: Promotes equity through support to LMICs and intergenerational equity.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Grounds action in socio-ecological balance connecting integrity to well-being.
Stewardship: Emphasizes ecosystem restoration and safe wildlife management.
Transdisciplinarity: Institutionalizes coordination via focal points and inclusive governance.
governanceRole: Operationalizes linkages across GBF targets. Formalizes One Health governance structures (interministerial). Promotes inclusive implementation.
limitations: Resource/capacity gaps not mitigated by designated funds. Limited integration with public health system mandates.
provisions: Decision 1: Adopts GAP. Decision 3: Encourages national implementation. Annex 12/13: Aligns OH actions with GBF Targets regarding governance and land use.

instrument: Provisional Voluntary Code of Conduct on the Sustainable Management of Plastics in Agriculture
description: Guides sustainable management of agricultural plastics across their lifecycle, aiming to reduce environmental/health risks and leakage.
principles: Equity: Calls for fair participation of vulnerable groups and smallholder farmers.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Addresses plastic pollution impacts on soil properties and biodiversity.
Stewardship: Promotes stewardship through the 6R model.
Transdisciplinarity: Encourages multistakeholder collaboration across sectors.
governanceRole: Establishes a cross-sectoral policy framework linking plastic management to OH. Promotes evidence-building. Supports national technical cooperation.
limitations: Meant to complement, not preempt, future legally binding plastic treaties. Non-binding reporting without formal compliance mechanisms.
provisions: Article 2.1: Objectives regarding protection from plastic pollution. Article 4.6.1: R&D on microplastics. Article 5.2.2: Alternatives assessment.
interlinkages: Basel Convention, International Code of Conduct on Pesticide Management

instrument: WOAH One Health Strategy
description: Roadmap embedding One Health within veterinary services, highlighting coordination and workforce capacity to manage zoonoses, AMR, food, and environmental health.
principles: Equity: Advocates for veterinary inclusion in national health strategies.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Advances balance through ecosystem-informed surveillance.
Stewardship: Embeds stewardship through responsible antimicrobial use.
Transdisciplinarity: Fosters collaboration including environmental, public, and animal health.
governanceRole: Positions veterinary services as OH change-agents using MCM OT tools. Focuses on workforce competency. Promotes integrated data systems (WAHIS).
limitations: Environment sector engagement remains secondary. Resource constraints hinder implementation in LMICs. Not legally enforceable.
provisions: Governance Pillar: Endorses MCM OT. Workforce Pillar: Mandates competency training. Surveillance Pillar: Supports joint monitoring.
interlinkages: OH Joint Plan of Action, IHR

instrument: Global Action Plan on Climate Change and Health
description: Framework integrating health into climate policies via leadership, evidence, and capacity-building. Promotes climate-resilient, low-carbon health systems.
principles: Equity: Advances equity recognizing linkages across systems.
Inclusion: Strengthens inclusion of marginalized groups in climate planning.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Addresses environmental drivers of disease.
Stewardship: Embodies stewardship via resilient low-carbon systems.
Transdisciplinarity: Links health, environment, agriculture, and energy sectors.
governanceRole: Prioritizes equity. Promotes intersectoral One Health integration. Strengthens research and data systems. Provides capacity-building guidance.
limitations: Resource dependence on external funding. Coordination complexity may slow progress. Nationally determined actions risk uneven uptake.
provisions: Leadership Action Area: Integrate health into climate plans. Evidence Area: Strengthen surveillance. Capacity-building Area: Resilient systems and finance.

instrument: Global strategy for the prevention and control of high pathogenic avian influenza
description: Ten-year roadmap to reduce impacts of HPAI via a OH systems approach. Focuses on prevention, protection, and transformation of poultry value chains.
principles: Equity: Promotes shared responsibility across sectors.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Recognizes ecological dynamics in managing spillover.
Stewardship: Advances sustainable transformation of poultry systems.
Transdisciplinarity: Operationalizes coordination via multi-level governance.
governanceRole: Anchors OH in animal disease control. Strengthens joint surveillance/data-sharing. Builds institutional capacity via task forces and steering committees.
limitations: National funding uneven (LMICs lack budgets). Limited operational inclusion of public health authorities outside outbreak response.
provisions: Objective 1: OH approach to prevent spillover. Output 3.1: Transform poultry systems via participatory processes. Output 1.1: Integrated surveillance.
interlinkages: IHR, PIP Framework, Terrestrial Animal Health Code

instrument: Ramsar Resolution IX.23: Highly pathogenic avian influenza and its consequences for wetland and waterbird conservation
description: Recognizes HPAI risks, rejects lethal control/habitat destruction, and calls for coordinated, multisectoral response emphasizing ecosystem-based management.
principles: Equity: Highlights vulnerability of rural livelihoods and LMICs.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Positions biodiversity monitoring as buffer against disease emergence.
Stewardship: Advocates ecological stewardship over reactive disease control.
Transdisciplinarity: Promotes intersectoral governance linking health, agriculture, and conservation.
governanceRole: Encourages safe land use rejecting culling. Calls for integrated contingency planning. Promotes cooperation with FAO, WHO, WOAH, and CMS.
limitations: Health and veterinary integration relies on voluntary proactive national participation. Scientific uncertainty regarding transmission pathways.
provisions: Para 16: Integrated planning. Para 17-18: Rejects lethal control. Para 21-23: Urges capacity-building. Para 24: Coordination with technical partners.
interlinkages: Ramsar, IHR, WHO Pandemic Agreement, PIP Framework, CMS Res 14/18

instrument: Ramsar Resolution VIII.18 Invasive species and wetlands
description: Addresses IAS threats to wetlands, calling for national risk assessments, rapid response, and policy harmonization with CBD and IUCN.
principles: Equity: Acknowledges uneven national capacities for IAS monitoring.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Frames IAS as disruptors that increase disease vulnerability.
Stewardship: Embeds prevention to preserve wetland integrity.
Transdisciplinarity: Encourages collaboration with multiple institutions.
governanceRole: Integrates IAS control into national policies. Promotes early detection and transboundary coordination. Includes aquatic/terrestrial invasions.
limitations: Relies on national reporting and voluntary alignment. Training and capacity-building are encouraged but not resourced.
provisions: Para 16: Risk assessments. Para 22: Cooperation across transboundary wetlands. Para 24: Harmonize with MEAs. Para 26: Regional awareness programs.
interlinkages: Ramsar Convention, CBD, CITES Res Conf 13.10

instrument: Ramsar Resolution VIII.3: Climate change and wetlands: impacts, adaptation, and mitigation
description: Highlights dual role of wetlands regarding climate change. Urges integration of wetland resilience and carbon storage into strategies, preventing ecological damage from mitigation.
principles: Inclusion: Recognizes risks to vulnerable communities dependent on wetlands.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Grounds linkages in biodiversity and ecosystem service resilience.
Stewardship: Emphasizes peatland restoration and resilience-based planning.
Transdisciplinarity: Calls for coordinated planning across UNFCCC, CBD, and IPCC.
governanceRole: Links climate vulnerability to disease and disaster. Promotes wetland-based adaptation. Encourages collaboration with climate science bodies.
limitations: Limited explicit public health framing. Lacks integration with ministries of health or disease monitoring systems.
provisions: Para 15: Wetland management to reduce climate risk. Para 16: Peatland protection. Para 17-19: Integrate Ramsar into UNFCCC accounting.

instrument: Ramsar Resolution XI.12: Wetlands and health: taking an ecosystem approach
description: Defines wetlands as central to health. Embraces OH/EcoHealth frameworks, calling for integrated management to address disease risks and well-being.
principles: Equity: Recognizes wetlands' role supporting vulnerable/Indigenous populations.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Connects biodiversity loss and contamination to poor health.
Stewardship: Advocates for ecosystem-based disease prevention.
Transdisciplinarity: Promotes whole-of-landscape planning and dialogue.
governanceRole: Endorses formal ecosystem approaches to health. Promotes Ramsar technical reports for integrated risk assessments. Supports capacity building.
limitations: Health system integration depends on national interpretation. Disease linkages require specific policy alignment.
provisions: Para 11-12: Wetlands as key for public health. Para 29: Urges ecosystem-based management. Para 30-31: Calls for Wetland Disease Manual usage.

instrument: WOAH Resolution 27: The 'One Health' Approach to Address Health Risks at the Animal Human Ecosystem Interface
description: Promotes integrated OH governance by linking human, animal, and ecosystem health. Underscores veterinary roles in zoonoses, AMR, and food safety.
principles: Equity: Promotes equity by encouraging cooperation across sectors.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Emphasizes interconnectedness of humans, animals, and ecosystems.
Stewardship: Calls for preventive, sustainable health policies protecting animal welfare.
Transdisciplinarity: Urges integrated responses involving various knowledge systems.
governanceRole: Promotes cross-sectoral coordination platforms. Encourages risk-based policy design. Strengthens integrated surveillance efforts.
limitations: Fragmented veterinary and environmental integration. Veterinary authorities often lack formal mandates in intersectoral platforms. Incompatible data sharing.
provisions: Para 4: Advocates for OH approaches and capacity building. Para 5: Encourages use of WOAH PVS Tool. Para 8: Incorporate OH in curricula.
interlinkages: OH Joint Plan of Action, IHR, WHO Pandemic Agreement, WOAH OH Strategy

instrument: Conference Resolution 4/2015: Antimicrobial Resistance
description: Commits FAO to global AMR response using OH approach linking agriculture and health. Urges national strategies and multisectoral cooperation.
principles: Equity: Promotes shared responsibility across sectors.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Highlights ecological drivers of AMR like contamination.
Stewardship: Encourages sustainable antimicrobial use in food systems.
Transdisciplinarity: Formalizes collaboration through Quadripartite.
governanceRole: Anchors AMR within FAO mandate. Supports national action plans. Integrates AMR into food safety and surveillance systems.
limitations: Limited operational detail on environmental implementation. Voluntary nature weakens accountability. Narrow focus on food/ag sectors.
provisions: Para 6: Recognizes OH need. OP 1: Endorses FAO Action Plan. OP 2: Urges multisectoral national strategies.
interlinkages: WHO Global Action Plan on AMR, WOAH Strategy on AMR

instrument: UNEA Resolution 2/16: Mainstreaming of biodiversity for well-being
description: Calls on governments to integrate biodiversity into national policy aligned with 2030 Agenda. Encourages cross-sectoral collaboration for well-being.
principles: Equity: Advocates equity through country-specific approaches.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Reinforces balance integrating conservation into food/tourism.
Stewardship: Embodies stewardship promoting sustainable resource use.
Transdisciplinarity: Encourages cross-sectoral governance.
governanceRole: Supports biodiversity mainstreaming across development sectors. Aligns with SDGs. Builds political momentum.
limitations: Focuses on planning over implementation lacking concrete execution guidance.
provisions: OP 1: Recognizes CBD COP-13 theme. OP 2: Alignment with 2030 Agenda. OP 3: Integration into national development sectors.
interlinkages: CBD, GBF, GAP for Biodiversity and Health

instrument: UNEA Resolution 3/4: Environment and Health
description: Comprehensively addresses interlinkages between environment and health, promoting integrated governance and risk management.
principles: Equity: Promotes equity via support for developing countries.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Recognizes structural threats to health/ecosystems.
Stewardship: Emphasizes prevention and life-cycle approaches.
Transdisciplinarity: Embeds transdisciplinary action across diverse sectors.
governanceRole: Operationalizes OH across clusters. Expands evidence base with WHO/FAO/WOAH. Promotes multisectoral coordination platforms.
limitations: No formal intersectoral mandates. Limited compliance tracking. Funding constraints for LMICs.
provisions: OP 24: OH approach across domains. OP 25-27: Biodiversity-health integration. OP 29-35: OH-based AMR governance.
interlinkages: CBD, GBF, GAP for Biodiversity and Health

instrument: Conference Resolution 6/2019: Antimicrobial Resistance
description: Reaffirms FAO's AMR leadership, endorsing Quadripartite collaboration, urging surveillance/prudent use, and supporting LMICs.
principles: Equity: Promotes shared responsibilities across domains.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Recognizes environmental contamination as AMR driver.
Stewardship: Emphasizes responsible use and sustainable practices.
Transdisciplinarity: Strengthens joint AMR governance through Quadripartite.
governanceRole: Endorses expanded Tripartite/UNEP framework. Aligns with WHO GAP. Prioritizes support for LMICs.
limitations: Lacks clarity on operationalizing environmental surveillance. No structured roles for civil society.
provisions: OP 1: Supports Tripartite work. OP 4: Establish coordination for WHO GAP. OP 7: Support for developing countries.
interlinkages: WHO GAP on AMR, WOAH Strategy on AMR

instrument: Resolution 14: OIE's Engagement in the One Health Global Effort to Control Antimicrobial Resistance
description: Strengthens global coordination for AMR via OH approach, focusing on action plans, Tripartite coordination, and sustainable investments.
principles: Equity: Promotes veterinary roles in multisectoral efforts.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Recognizes AMR as threat to balance.
Stewardship: Calls for behavioral change in agricultural practices.
Transdisciplinarity: Coordinates global cross-sector monitoring efforts.
governanceRole: Promotes antimicrobial stewardship. Supports ANIMUSE database for harmonized surveillance. Capacity building in veterinary governance.
limitations: Limited regulation of antimicrobials in animal sectors. Inconsistent reporting. Insufficient enforcement capacity in some countries.
provisions: Para 3: Reaffirms commitment to NAPs. Para 4: ANIMUSE reporting. Para 9: Urges contributions to Partner Fund for LMICs.
interlinkages: WHO GAP on AMR, WOAH Strategy on AMR, Codex CXC 61-2005

instrument: WHA 73.5: Strengthening efforts on food safety
description: Reaffirms food safety as core to health. Calls for OH approach integrating health, agriculture, trade, and environment policies.
principles: Equity: Integrates food safety into national multi-sector policies.
Inclusion: Advocates for sustainability and access for all.
Stewardship: Promotes responsible investment in safety systems.
Transdisciplinarity: Emphasizes coordinated global governance.
governanceRole: Promotes OH cross-sector collaboration. Calls for health-in-all-policies. Advocates for Codex usage and WHO/FAO collaboration.
limitations: Focus remains largely on national governments with less explicit integration of communities. Implementation varies by capacity.
provisions: Preamble: OH approach includes managing risks along food chain. OP 1(3): Urges cross-sector collaboration and sustainability.
interlinkages: Codex CXS 193-1995, Codex CXC 1-1969, WTO SPS

instrument: WHA 74.7: Strengthening WHO preparedness for and response to health emergencies
description: Roadmap for strengthening emergency capacities. Calls for OH collaboration, improved surveillance, and equitable access to tools.
principles: Equity: Emphasizes collaborative preparedness across domains.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Links emergencies to environmental disruption.
Stewardship: Calls for proactive stewardship and long-term resilience.
Transdisciplinarity: Advances formal collaboration among Quadripartite agencies.
governanceRole: Institutionalizes OH coordination globally. Integrates surveillance (GLEWS). Supports country-led multisectoral preparedness.
limitations: Human health remains dominant frame. Operational specificity lacking. Member State focus may sideline non-state expertise.
provisions: OP 7(3): All-hazard OH approach. OP 8-10: Reform GLEWS, establish common strategy on OH with partners.
interlinkages: IHR, WHO Pandemic Agreement, PIP Framework

instrument: UNEA Resolultion 5/6: Biodiversity and Health
description: Recognizes interlinkages between biodiversity and well-being. Emphasizes OH in preventing pandemics and supports cross-policy integration.
principles: Equity: Support for developing countries in OH implementation.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Re-centers ecosystem services as foundational to health.
Stewardship: Supports intergenerational stewardship.
Transdisciplinarity: Calls for transdisciplinary approaches.
governanceRole: Promotes capacity building in LMICs. Aligns biodiversity with zoonotic prevention. Highlights risks during spillover events.
limitations: Health sector engagement is advisory. Lacks measurable benchmarks for integration progress.
provisions: OP 2: Mainstream biodiversity-health linkages. OP 5: Reduce spillover via sustainable use. OP 13: Highlights AMR priority.

instrument: WHA 75.13: Global strategy on infection prevention and control
description: Mandates development of global strategy on IPC to reduce healthcare infections and AMR, aligning with WASH and OH frameworks.
principles: Equity: Calls for IPC measures across all settings.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Recognizes interplay of health, WASH, and environment.
Stewardship: Advocates science-based IPC preventing harm.
Transdisciplinarity: Aligns IPC with AMR, safety, and environmental programs.
governanceRole: Integrates IPC with AMR/WASH. Emphasizes workforce development. Establishes measurable implementation frameworks.
limitations: Weak IPC presence outside hospitals disrupts coordination. Fragmented HAI data. IPC professionals lack structural authority.
provisions: OP3: Ensure functional IPC programmes taking into account OH approach. OP6: Ensure sustainable IPC/WASH infrastructures. OP2: Translate strategy into action plan.

instrument: WHA 76.17: The impact of chemicals, waste and pollution on human health
description: Calls for commitments to the WHO Global Strategy to address risks of plastics, chemicals, and waste via cross-sector engagement.
principles: Socio-ecological equilibrium: Acknowledges harmful effects of pollution on ecosystems.
Stewardship: Promotes policies reducing pollution sustainably.
Transdisciplinarity: Encourages cooperation among health and environment authorities.
governanceRole: Strengthens biomonitoring systems. Institutionalizes multisector governance via Global Framework on Chemicals. Aligns pollution policy with health goals.
limitations: Fragmented governance across sectors. Weak national biomonitoring systems. Limited health sector engagement in pollution policy.
provisions: Para 1: Take impact of chemicals into account. Para 4: Requests OH research linkages regarding pollution/waste.

instrument: CMS Resolution 12.6: Wildlife health & migratory species
description: Affirms interdependence of wildlife, human, and ecosystem health. Emphasizes OH-based governance and non-lethal responses.
principles: Equity: Encourages support to low-income countries.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Defines healthy ecosystems as determinants of resilience.
Stewardship: Emphasizes ecosystem-based prevention and non-lethal response.
Transdisciplinarity: Strengthens cross-border collaboration among agencies.
governanceRole: Recognizes environmental drivers of disease. Advocates upstream non-lethal management. Consolidates previous resolutions.
limitations: No formal compliance framework. Health sector roles are supportive rather than institutionalized. Data limitations in Global South.
provisions: Preamble: Recognizes full suite of drivers. Para 4: Non-lethal science-based responses. Para 5: Links wildlife health to OH goals.

instrument: CMS Resolution 14/18: Avian influenza
description: Addresses HPAI threat to birds, ecosystems, and humans via OH approach. Rejects culling/habitat destruction.
principles: Equity: Recognizes inequities and calls for global support.
Socio-ecological equilibrium: Frames intact ecosystems as buffers against emergence.
Stewardship: Opposes destructive responses calling for biosecurity.
Transdisciplinarity: Institutionalizes cross-border coordination.
governanceRole: Formally applies OH lens to HPAI outbreak response. Rejects harmful wildlife control. Establishes conservation-driven surveillance.
limitations: Implementation is voluntary. Human health agencies are not mandated implementers. Limited guidance on integrating surveillance.
provisions: Para 1: National HPAI contingency plans. Para 2: Avoids culling. Para 3: Multisectoral spillover measures. Para 4: Surveillance and data-sharing.
interlinkages: CMS, Ramsar, IHR, PIP Framework, Terrestrial Animal Health Code

instrument: Resolution Conf. 10.21 (Rev. CoP19): Transport of live specimens
description: Guidelines for humane, health-conscious transport of CITES-listed species, adopting IATA standards to minimize stress and disease transmission.
principles: Equity: Promotes safety in trade via standardized protocols.
Stewardship: Advances stewardship by minimizing transport cruelty/harm.
Transdisciplinarity: Encourages coordination between CITES, IATA, WOAH.
governanceRole: Codifies health safeguards in logistics. Recognizes disease risks linked to handling. Encourages expert collaboration.
limitations: Focus on conservation over integrated disease surveillance. Relies on national legislation. Voluntary adoption lacks accountability.
provisions: Preamble Para 8: Stress increases disease risk. Rec 2: Use IATA standards. Rec 3(d): Investigate high-mortality shipments.

instrument: Resolution Conf. 13.10 (Rev. CoP14): Trade in invasive alien species
description: Acknowledges trade in live animals/plants contributes to IAS spread. Recommends incorporating IAS risks into permitting and CBD collaboration.
principles: Socio-ecological equilibrium: Accounts for ecosystem vulnerability in live trade.
Stewardship: Calls for precaution in trade affecting shared ecosystems.
Transdisciplinarity: Promotes inter-convention cooperation (CITES-CBD).
governanceRole: Integrates IAS prevention into trade governance. Promotes risk consultation between states. Strengthens CITES/CBD cooperation.
limitations: No explicit integration of public health/veterinary sectors. Relies on national capacity to regulate risk.
provisions: Rec 1(a): Consider IAS risks in legislation. Rec 1(b): Exporters consult importers. Rec 1(c): Synergy between CITES and CBD.
